metadata.file_name: 92. Park et al. (2025). Measurement Invariance for Multilingual Learners Using Item Response and Response Time in PISA 2018.pdf
metadata.title: Measurement Invariance for Multilingual Learners Using Item Response and Response Time in PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for the United States and restricts the analytic sample to 15-year-old students with available item-level response data across reading, mathematics, and science. The authors further restrict the item set to those available in the PISA database for scored responses (511 total items) and response-time variables (423 items), and they classify students into ML vs non-ML using the home-language questionnaire item. The paper does not report applying PISA complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures in the DIF and response-time invariance analyses; instead, it relies on IRT-based estimation (including WLE for latent ability) and model-based item-fit statistics. Because the manuscript does not specify weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate methods, readers should treat the results as conditional on the analyzed sample and consider re-running with official PISA weights if population-representative inference is required.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scores; the study focuses on measurement invariance using multigroup IRT item-fit statistics (RMSD/MD) and response-time functioning (LOWESS and DRT) between multilingual learners and non-MLs. As a result, plausible-value generation/combining is not part of the analysis pipeline. The manuscript also does not describe how missing item responses or missing response-time observations were handled when forming the 511 scored items and 423 response-time items, which is a reporting gap for transparency about the analytic sample construction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 data for the United States and analyzed 15-year-old students. Students were classified as multilingual learners (ML) vs non-ML based on the questionnaire item “What language do you speak at home most of the time,” where “language of the test” indicates non-ML and “Other languages” indicates ML. The study used all available items within reading, mathematics, and science generated from the PISA database (511 scored items total) and a subset with available item-level response times (423 items), with item types including computer-scored (multiple-choice and constructed responses) and human-coded constructed responses.

main_findings.target_variable: Differential item functioning (DIF) for scored responses (RMSD/MD)
main_findings.performance_metrics: DIF prevalence: 13.66% of overall items (50/366) for ML; 12.81% of computer-scored items (36/281) and 16.47% of human-coded items (14/85). DIF thresholding used RMSD = 0.12 for cognitive domains; MD indicated 50% of all items had negative MD for ML. Among DIF items, 22/50 (44%) had negative MD for ML.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for the United States, the study leveraged home language (ML vs non-ML) to evaluate differential item functioning for scored responses, finding that a non-trivial share of reading items showed DIF for ML students (13.66% overall; more DIF among computer-scored and human-coded items). This indicates that reading items in PISA 2018 are not fully measurement-equivalent across home-language groups, suggesting test developers and educators should review and potentially adapt construct-irrelevant linguistic demands in reading tasks for multilingual learners.

main_findings.target_variable: Latent ability differences after releasing DIF constraints (WLE-based θ)
main_findings.performance_metrics: WLE latent ability comparison: non-ML > ML in reading, t(4,778) = 6.51, p < .001, d = 0.26 (small effect).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for the United States, the study leveraged home language (ML vs non-ML) to compare WLE-based latent ability estimates after releasing DIF-identified item-parameter constraints, finding that non-ML students had significantly higher latent reading ability than ML students (d = 0.26). This indicates that even when DIF items are accounted for, multilingual learners still show lower estimated reading proficiency, implying that equity-oriented supports (e.g., language scaffolding and time/resources) may be needed alongside item fairness checks.

main_findings.performance_metrics: DRT critical exceedances: 18 items (8%) in reading exceeded the critical value of 1.96. DRT effect size range: (−8.36, 42.59). Positive DRT indicates MLs spent more time than non-MLs; overall direction was skewed against ML students.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for the United States, the study leveraged home language (ML vs non-ML) to test differential response time functioning, finding that a subset of reading items showed significant DRT effects (8% exceeding 1.96) with effect sizes indicating ML students generally spent more time on items matched on ability. This indicates that time-on-task differences may reflect language-related processing demands, suggesting that providing additional time or language supports could improve fairness without necessarily changing the underlying construct.

main_findings.target_variable: Differential item functioning (DIF) for scored responses (RMSD/MD)
main_findings.performance_metrics: DIF prevalence: 7.14% of total items (5/70) for ML; 5.77% of computer-scored items (3/52) and 11.11% of human-coded response items (2/18). DIF thresholding used RMSD = 0.12 for cognitive domains; MD indicated 49% of all items had negative MD for ML. Among DIF items, 1/5 (20%) had negative MD for ML. Additional analysis (Latent ability differences after releasing DIF constraints (WLE-based θ)): WLE latent ability comparison: non-ML > ML in mathematics, t(2,594) = 4.19, p < .001, d = 0.23 (small effect). ANCOVA controlling for reading: group difference in math becomes non-significant after controlling for reading scores.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data for the United States, the study leveraged home language (ML vs non-ML) to evaluate differential item functioning for scored responses, finding that mathematics showed the lowest DIF proportion among the three domains (7.14% overall) and that DIF items were concentrated with higher RMSD values for ML students. This indicates that mathematics items are comparatively more measurement-equivalent than reading and science, but still contain a subset where multilingual learners experience different item characteristics, motivating targeted item review rather than wholesale test redesign.

main_findings.performance_metrics: DRT critical exceedances: 7 items (10%) in mathematics exceeded the critical value of 1.96. DRT effect size range: (−12.61, 42.68). Positive DRT values were most prevalent in mathematics (89% of items with positive DRT).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Mathematics data for the United States, the study leveraged home language (ML vs non-ML) to test differential response time functioning, finding that mathematics had a relatively high proportion of significant DRT items (10%) and that most positive DRT effects indicated ML students were slower than non-ML students at matched ability. This indicates that even where mathematics score differences may be explained by reading, response-time bias can still disadvantage multilingual learners, supporting time/resource accommodations and item-format review.

main_findings.target_variable: Differential item functioning (DIF) for scored responses (RMSD/MD)
main_findings.performance_metrics: DIF prevalence: 11% of items (13/115) for ML; 13.25% of computer-scored items (11/83) and 6.25% of human-coded response items (2/32). DIF thresholding used RMSD = 0.12 for cognitive domains; MD indicated 49% of all items had negative MD for ML. Among DIF items, 9/13 (69%) had negative MD for ML. Additional analysis (Latent ability differences after releasing DIF constraints (WLE-based θ)): WLE latent ability comparison: non-ML > ML in science, t(2,588) = 7.18, p < .001, d = 0.39 (small effect). ANCOVA controlling for reading: science group difference remains significant, F(1, 2,578) = 18.53, p < .001.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science data for the United States, the study leveraged home language (ML vs non-ML) to evaluate differential item functioning for scored responses, finding that science had a moderate DIF proportion (11%) with DIF items more often showing negative MD for ML (69%), consistent with ML items being comparatively easier for ML students. This indicates that science assessment validity for multilingual learners may be affected by item-level linguistic/cultural features, supporting item-level diagnostics and potential language-sensitive revisions.

main_findings.performance_metrics: DRT critical exceedances: 8 items (7%) in science exceeded the critical value of 1.96. DRT effect size range: (−6.82, 41.52). Positive DRT values were prevalent in science (85% of items with positive DRT).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science data for the United States, the study leveraged home language (ML vs non-ML) to test differential response time functioning, finding significant DRT effects for a subset of items (7% exceeding 1.96) with positive DRT effects indicating ML students generally spent more time than non-ML students at matched ability. This indicates that science assessment fairness for multilingual learners is also affected by processing-time demands, implying that assessment accommodations and language-sensitive item development may be necessary.

data.outcome_summary: This study investigates assessment bias for multilingual learners in PISA 2018 within the United States by combining multigroup IRT DIF analysis for scored responses with response-time invariance testing. Using 4,838 students and 511 scored items (reading: 366; math: 70; science: 115) plus 423 items with response-time data, the authors detect DIF using RMSD thresholds (0.12 for cognitive domains) and estimate latent abilities using WLE after releasing DIF-identified item constraints. Non-ML students show higher latent ability than ML students in reading (d = 0.26), mathematics (d = 0.23), and science (d = 0.39), with math gaps disappearing after controlling for reading while science gaps remain significant (F(1, 2,578) = 18.53). Across domains, ML students generally spend more time than non-ML students at matched ability, with DRT significant for subsets of items (reading 8%, math 10%, science 7%). The paper does not report survey-weight usage or missing-data handling, and it uses measurement invariance diagnostics rather than predictive ML, so causal claims about language effects cannot be inferred.
